analysis.one_liner: Bans a list of toxic chemicals, including PFAS and bisphenols, from food packaging.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2026 with 14 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not acted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal food safety law to declare that a specific list of chemicals cannot be used in anything that touches food, including packaging. The banned list covers whole classes of chemicals such as ortho-phthalates and PFAS, plus named substances like bisphenol A, formaldehyde, benzene, asbestos, and styrene polymers. The ban would take effect two years after enactment, and states would remain free to pass stricter rules of their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats packaged food, since the chemicals listed are used in grease-resistant wrappers, can linings, plasticizers, and processing equipment and can migrate into food. Children, pregnant women, and workers are explicitly named as populations regulators must consider when weighing substitutes, because they face disproportionate exposure or harm.

how_it_helps.text: Deems 15 groups of chemicals unsafe for use as food contact substances under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, including all ortho-phthalates, all PFAS, the bisphenol family (A, B, S, F, AF), acrylamide, BHA, asbestos, benzene, formaldehyde, and styrene polymers.

Requires the FDA to consider potential adverse effects on vulnerable populations, defined to include infants, children, pregnant women, the elderly, people with preexisting conditions, exposed workers, and overburdened communities, when judging any substitute chemical a company proposes.
Preserves the right of states and cities to adopt stricter food packaging rules than the federal standard, including outright prohibitions.
Gives food packaging makers and food companies two years after enactment before the ban applies, to reformulate products.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical makers that produce phthalates, PFAS, and bisphenols, and the packaging and food companies that would have to reformulate products or find substitutes, with some of those costs likely passed to consumers in the price of packaged goods.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans entire chemical classes by name rather than letting the FDA judge each use case by case, so some specific uses that pose little risk would be swept up in a flat prohibition, and substitutes are not guaranteed to be safer or as effective.

PFAS and similar chemicals provide grease and water resistance in food packaging; eliminating them entirely may force costlier alternatives and raise packaging costs, some portion of which would reach shoppers.
A two-year compliance deadline is tight for supply chains that source packaging globally, which could create transition costs for smaller food producers in particular.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit, reducing migration of well-studied hazardous chemicals into food, falls on the general public, while the reformulation cost falls on a specific set of manufacturers and only partially on consumers. The main design weakness is the breadth of the ban: a class-wide prohibition is simpler to enforce but blunter than chemical-by-chemical review, and the bill leans on regulators to vet substitutes for vulnerable populations rather than proving each substitute safe up front.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action since June 2026.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on June 9, 2026, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors, all in the House.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action appears in the record.
No version of the bill has received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, chemical producers and food packaging manufacturers, whose products remain unrestricted while the bill sits without action in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical and packaging makers, for now

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: 14 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican cosponsors signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters are Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill bans all PFAS and other listed chemical classes from food contact uses, eliminating a market for these producers. Ordinary people gain reduced chemical exposure, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.
Packaging makers would have to reformulate or replace grease-resistant and plastic packaging within two years. Consumers bear only the pass-through of any added cost, while gaining safer packaging.
Food companies rely on listed chemicals in can linings, wrappers, and processing; the ban forces reformulation. Cost increases would be partially passed to shoppers.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action months after referral, no Republican support, and a crowded Energy and Commerce agenda in the final year of the Congress, the bill is likely to die in committee without a vote, the usual fate for a one-party food safety bill of this kind.
